newsitem.title: CANADA: Canada's Goodale to resume CWB change if reelected.
newsitem.headline: Canada's Goodale to resume CWB change if reelected.

text.p: A bill amending the way one of the world's oldest and largest state commodity export monopolies operates will be reintroduced into Canada's Parliament if the governing Liberal Party is re-elected, Canadian Agriculture Minister Ralph Goodale said.

"The legislation that we had before Parliament in the last session, that is legislation we will pick up immediately after this election," Goodale told reporters at a live television election press conference in Regina.
Canadian Prime Minister Jean Chretien launched the federal election campaign on April 27 for a June 2 vote.

"It would accomplish those goals of more democracy, more accountability, more flexibility, more responsiveness and more power than ever before by farmers themselves in directing and controlling the activities of the Canadian Wheat Board" he said.

Goodale introduced amendments to the CWB Act on December 3, 1996, which proposed to modernize the CWB's governance to a farmer-elected board of directors from the current government appointed commissioners.
The CWB, Canada's fifth largest exporter, made C$5.8 billion in wheat and barley sales in the 1995/96 crop year (Aug/July).
Canada is the second largest seller of wheat to the world.
The amendments, which were before the last session of Parliament but were not passed into law prior to Chretien's election call, also would have allowed the CWB to make cash grain purchases.
Price pooling, or one price for all farmers, was a founding principle of the CWB when it was formed in 1935.
The amendments would also allow the CWB to expedite adjustment payments to farmers, terminate pool accounts at any time and make early payouts to farmers.

Under those proposed amendments the CWB would also have been allowed to issue negotiable producer certificates, defray farmers' storage and carrying costs, facilitate deliveries to condominium-type storage and use on-farm mobile elevators to receive deliveries.
